summary:
Quick sort with a **three-way partition**: one pass splits the range into values below the pivot, equal to it,
and above it, and the equal block is finished on the spot. With few distinct values, each pass removes a whole
value from the problem, so repeats make it faster, not slower. O(n log n) expected, O(n · distinct) at worst
under few-distinct data.

question.md:
Sort `readings` without the built-in sort. Most readings repeat a handful of values.

- **Up to 10⁵ readings**, possibly all equal.
- The statement warns that a quick sort which ignores repeats becomes very slow.

**Edge cases to keep in mind**

- All readings equal: a two-way quick sort degrades to O(n²) and n-deep recursion.
- Only a few distinct values: most of the work should be skipped.
- The built-in sort isn't allowed.

think.md:
**Why O(n log n) sorts work.** Insertion sort places each value by scanning a sorted prefix: up to `n` steps per value,
O(n²) total. The O(n log n) sorts **divide** the problem:

- **Merge sort** splits the array in half, sorts each half, and merges two sorted halves in linear time. There are
  `log₂ n` levels of halving and each level does O(n) merging: O(n log n), always. It's **stable** (equal values keep
  their order) but needs an O(n) buffer for arrays.
- **Quick sort** picks a pivot, partitions the values into "smaller" and "larger" around it, then sorts both sides. With
  a random pivot the split is balanced on average: O(n log n) expected, in place, but O(n²) if pivots keep being
  extreme, and not stable.

**What goes wrong with repeats.** Two-way partitioning puts values equal to the pivot on one side. When almost
everything equals the pivot, each partition removes only the pivot itself: `n` levels of O(n) work.

**Three-way partitioning.** Split into `< pivot | = pivot | > pivot`. The middle block is already in its final
place and is never touched again, so a value repeated many times is handled in one pass. The loop is the Dutch
national flag: `lt` ends the "less" zone, `i` scans, `gt` starts the "greater" zone.

idea.md: Quick sort with a random pivot and two-way partitioning (`< pivot` on the left, everything else on the right).

lines.text: Random pivot, then everything strictly smaller moves left. Copies of the pivot all stay on the right side.
Recurse. With many copies, the right side shrinks by only one element per level.

complexity.md: **Time O(n²)** when most values are equal (each partition peels off one value). **Space O(n)** recursion in that case.

steps.text: Positions 0..6: pivot 5 lands at 3; the 3 other copies of 5 still have to be sorted on the right.
Positions 0..2: pivot 3 lands at 1; the 1 other copies of 3 still have to be sorted on the right.
Positions 4..6: pivot 5 lands at 4; the 2 other copies of 5 still have to be sorted on the right.
Positions 5..6: pivot 5 lands at 5; the 1 other copies of 5 still have to be sorted on the right.
Sorted, but every copy of 5 needed its own partition pass: [1, 3, 3, 5, 5, 5, 5].

walk.title: Two-way quick sort: values smaller than the pivot go left, everything else right. Equal values all pile onto one side.

limits.md: Equal values keep landing on the same side. Grouping them into their own block removes them from further work.

approaches.title: Three-way quick sort

idea.md:
Three-way quick sort with an explicit stack: partition `[lo, hi]` into `< p`, `= p`, `> p` with `lt`, `i`,
`gt`, then push only `[lo, lt − 1]` and `[gt + 1, hi]`.

**Why it's fast with repeats.** With `d` distinct values, each value becomes the pivot's equal block once,
so the work is about O(n log d) expected.

build: Push the less and greater ranges only.

notes.python: An explicit stack of ranges instead of recursion (Python's recursion limit is low).

lines.text: A random pivot value; `lt`, `i` and `gt` mark the three regions.
Smaller values go to the front block, bigger ones to the back block, equal ones stay in the middle. A value swapped in from `gt` hasn't been looked at yet, so `i` doesn't advance then.
The equal block `[lt, gt]` is done; only the smaller and bigger parts are sorted further.

complexity.md: **Time O(n log n)** expected, O(n log d) with `d` distinct values. **Space O(log n)** expected stack.

steps.text: Pivot 5. lt, i and gt start at the ends.
a[i] was equal: leave it in the middle.
a[i] was smaller: swap it to the lt side.
a[i] was equal: leave it in the middle.
a[i] was smaller: swap it to the lt side.
a[i] was equal: leave it in the middle.
a[i] was smaller: swap it to the lt side.
a[i] was equal: leave it in the middle.
Every 5 sits in positions 3..6 and is done. Only the smaller side [3, 1, 3] still needs sorting.

walk.title: Three-way partition: one pass splits the range into < pivot | = pivot | > pivot, and the middle part is finished at once.

takeaways.md:
- **Many duplicates → three-way partition** (`<`, `=`, `>`).
- The equal block is final and skipped from then on.
- **Pitfall:** advancing `i` after swapping with `gt` (the arriving value is unexamined).
